title: Environment Setup
unlocks: A Linux machine that can compile C++.
objective: Get a working Linux toolchain on your Windows machine, learn just enough shell to move around in it, and compile and run one C++ program.
knows: nothing yet - this is the first stage
checks: g++ 11 or newer is installed and on your PATH.
git knows who you are (user.name and user.email are set).
The project configures cleanly, even though my-game/ is still empty.
hints: WSL2 is a real Ubuntu running alongside Windows, not an emulator. Install it from PowerShell with `wsl --install -d Ubuntu`, then reboot. Everything after that happens inside the Ubuntu terminal, not PowerShell.

Ubuntu ships without a compiler. The package that brings g++, make and friends is called `build-essential`. You also want `cmake`, `git`, `gdb` and `python3`. One `sudo apt install` line covers all of them.
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y build-essential gdb cmake git python3

Put the repository in your Linux home directory (`cd ~` then clone). If you work in /mnt/c the build will be roughly ten times slower and file permissions get strange, because that path crosses from Linux into Windows on every single file access.

prompts.title: My WSL2 install went wrong
prompts.body:
I am setting up WSL2 with Ubuntu on Windows so I can compile C++.

Here is what I ran:
<PASTE THE COMMAND>

Here is what it said:
<PASTE THE OUTPUT>

Walk me through what that message means before suggesting a fix, and tell me how I could have read it myself.

prompts.title: Explain this command before I run it
prompts.body:
Someone told me to run this command in Ubuntu:

<PASTE THE COMMAND>

Break it into its parts and explain what each one does. Tell me specifically whether it changes anything on my system permanently, and whether I should be careful with it. Do not just tell me it is safe.

prompts.title: Quiz me on the shell
prompts.body:
Quiz me on the handful of shell commands I need for this stage: pwd, ls, cd, mkdir, cat, less, which, and echo $?.

Ask me ONE question at a time and wait for my answer. Prefer questions like 'you are in /home/me and you want to get to /home/me/project/src, what do you type' over definition questions. If I get one wrong, do not give me the answer -- give me a smaller question that leads to it.
